Altitude And Circumcircle

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Move a triangle and watch three special dots: they always land on the circle through the corners; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag a corner, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the altitude lines, the equal lengths, point S and its circle.

Drag A, B or C, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

The circle through the three corners seems to know where the orthocenter will go: whenever H is reflected in a side, the new dot falls on that same circle.

Where the three dots come from

Each altitude meets the opposite side (or its extension) at a foot: Ha on BC, Hb on AC and Hc on AB. The altitude lines meet at H. The green dots are the reflections of H in those side lines: Ka = 2Ha − H, and likewise for b and c. The logic test checked all three against the circle for 4,006 triangles, including obtuse ones: every one lies on it.

Why the foot is halfway

Let Ka be the second point where the altitude AHa meets the circumcircle. The page's proof compares two angles: the right triangles CAHa and CBHb share the angle at C, so ∠CAHa = ∠CBHb; and the inscribed angles subtending the same arc CKa give ∠CAHa = ∠CBKa. Thus the altitude from B is both an altitude and an angle bisector in triangle BHKa, so it is also a median: HHa = HaKa. The page proves this for an acute triangle and notes that an obtuse angle needs a small change; the equality itself still held in every obtuse case we tested.

Four equal circles and equal arcs

Reflect the circumcircle in BC and it passes through H, B and C with the same radius; the reflection S of A in Ha lies on it too (AHa = HaS). The page adds that the circles through ABC, ABH, BCH and CAH are all equal — the test compared their radii for every triangle in the sample. It also says the arcs next to A each measure 2(90° − ∠BAC); that was confirmed for every acute triangle tested. For a right triangle H is a corner, so two of those four circles collapse onto a straight line.

Try dragging one corner past the opposite side to make an obtuse triangle: the green dots stay on the circle. Then tick Altitudes and Extra circle to see the second circle and the point S.
